excerpts.text: In November 2018, however, the redefinition of the ampere ― along with three other [SI base units](https://www.nist.gov/si-redefinition/definitions-si-base-units): the kilogram (mass), kelvin (temperature) and mole (amount of substance) ― was approved. Starting on May 20, 2019, the ampere is based on a fundamental physical constant: the elementary charge (e), which is the amount of electric charge in a single electron (negative) or proton (positive).

excerpts.text: The **ampere**[[note 1]](#cite_note-4) (symbol: **A**), [[4.1]](#cite_note-6) often [shortened](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clipping_(morphology) "Clipping (morphology)") to **amp**,[[note 2]](#cite_note-9) is the unit of [electric current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electric_current "Electric current") in the [International System of Units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_System_of_Units "International System of Units") (SI).
The [2019 revision of the SI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_revision_of_the_SI "2019 revision of the SI") redefined the ampere as follows:

The [international system of units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_system_of_units "International system of units") (SI) is based on seven [SI base units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SI_base_units "SI base units"): the second, metre, [kilogram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilogram "Kilogram"), [kelvin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin "Kelvin"), ampere, [mole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mole_(unit) "Mole (unit)"), and [candela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candela "Candela") – representing seven fundamental types of physical quantity, or ["dimensions"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimensional_analysis "Dimensional analysis") ([time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time "Time"), [length](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Length "Length"), [mass](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass "Mass"), [temperature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperature "Temperature"), electric current, [amount of substance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amount_of_substance "Amount of substance"), and [luminous intensity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luminous_intensity "Luminous intensity") respectively), with all other SI units being defined using these.

assessment.rationale: Span 214 lists the seven SI base units including ampere and kelvin separately, but does not state that kelvin is the base unit of electric current.
assessment.provenance_note: Spans list both units but no claimed relationship.
limitations: No span defines kelvin as electric current's base unit.

excerpts.text: When [Maxwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Clerk_Maxwell "James Clerk Maxwell") first introduced the concept of a coherent system, he identified three quantities that could be used as base units: mass, length, and time. [Giorgi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Giorgi "Giovanni Giorgi") later identified the need for an electrical base unit, for which the unit of electric current was chosen for SI. Another three base units (for temperature, amount of substance, and luminous intensity) were added later.[[1]](#cite_note-NIST330-1)
